name: Oral semaglutide (Rybelsus)
lead: Oral semaglutide, sold as Rybelsus, is a tablet form of the GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide. It was the first GLP-1 receptor agonist developed for oral administration, co-formulated with an absorption enhancer, sodium N-(8-[2-hydroxybenzoyl] amino) caprylate, that helps the peptide survive the stomach.[1]

People interested in fat loss and a leaner look follow it because semaglutide reduces appetite and body weight, and a tablet avoids injections. As body fat falls, facial fullness and body shape change. Rybelsus was approved in the US in September 2019 and in the EU in April 2020 for type 2 diabetes; in December 2025 the FDA approved an oral semaglutide for weight management under the Wegovy brand.[2]

Its use for weight loss in people without diabetes is discussed in appearance and fat-loss communities, where the pill is sometimes regarded as an alternative to injections. Trials in adults with overweight or obesity have tested 25 mg and 50 mg daily oral doses, and a Hacker News post linked a 2023 Novo Nordisk announcement of about 15 percent weight loss with the higher dose.[13][14][20] Wikipedia reports a phase III trial of injectable semaglutide in 1,961 adults with obesity found a mean weight change of -14.9% at week 68 versus -2.4% with placebo.[2]

paras: Rybelsus is indicated as an add-on therapy for adults with type 2 diabetes,[1] and a January 2023 label update allowed first-line use.[2] In October 2025 the FDA expanded its indication to reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events in high-risk adults with type 2 diabetes.[2]
Reviews of the pharmacology and clinical programme describe improvements in glycaemic control and body weight in people with type 2 diabetes.[1][3][4]

For weight loss without diabetes, the phase 3 OASIS 1 trial in the Lancet (2023) randomised adults with a BMI of at least 30, or at least 27 with weight-related complications, to oral semaglutide 50 mg daily or placebo,[13] and a 71-week New England Journal of Medicine trial (2025) tested a 25 mg dose in adults with overweight or obesity.[14] A randomised trial examined how oral semaglutide changed energy intake, appetite, control of eating and gastric emptying in adults with obesity,[16] and a registered phase 4 trial examines oral semaglutide for overweight or obesity.[5]

For cardiovascular outcomes, the SOUL trial of oral semaglutide in high-risk type 2 diabetes was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2025,[15] and a meta-analysis including SOUL and the FLOW kidney trial examined cardiovascular and kidney outcomes with long-acting injectable and oral GLP-1 agonists.[17]

Wikipedia's semaglutide page cites a 2024 systematic review of six studies in which lean body mass decreased in some cases, by 0 to 40 percent, while the ratio of lean to total body mass rose in all of them.[2]

The most common effects of semaglutide are nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, constipation and abdominal pain. The US label carries a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumours, and semaglutide is contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2.[2] A case report described reversible bilateral central scotoma associated with oral semaglutide.[6]
Wikipedia notes the common effects are dose-dependent and typically peak during the 8 to 12 week dose-escalation phase, and lists gallstones as a documented risk.[2]

Oral semaglutide has 94% homology with human GLP-1.[1] Because bioavailability by mouth is low compared with the injection (roughly 1 to 2% versus about 89%), the tablet is formulated with an absorption enhancer.[2][1]

According to Wikipedia, research on GLP-1 began in the 1970s, with Jens Juul Holst and Joel Habener reporting its significant effects in 1988, and Novo Nordisk's team developed liraglutide in 1998; semaglutide was later developed by a team including Jesper Lau, Thomas Kruse and Paw Bloch.[2] Rybelsus was approved in the US in September 2019 and in the EU in April 2020, a January 2023 label update allowed first-line use in adults with type 2 diabetes, and the FDA approved oral semaglutide for weight management under the Wegovy name in December 2025.[2] The European CHMP later recommended a new tablet form in several strengths.[2]

sections.h: Use in appearance and fat-loss communities
paras: Appearance-focused discussion of semaglutide centres on fat loss: lower body fat changes facial fullness, jaw and neck definition and body shape. A T Nation article asked whether semaglutide drugs are 'miracle fat-loss drugs' and noted public attention to celebrity use.[18] Bodybuilding forum members have also discussed combining semaglutide with other compounds, which is a separate topic with its own risks.[19]

A 2024 systematic review cited by Wikipedia reports lean body mass decreasing in some studies of semaglutide by 0 to 40 percent while the lean-to-total ratio rose in all of them, which is one reason muscle retention is a recurring theme among people who train.[2] Wikipedia also cites a 2025 systematic review finding people regained an average of 67% of lost weight in the year after stopping, returning to their previous weight on average within about a year and a half.[2]

Semaglutide became a widely discussed fat-loss drug. A T Nation article asked whether Ozempic, Wegovy and related drugs are miracle fat-loss drugs and noted that Elon Musk took semaglutide to get leaner and Kim Kardashian reportedly took it as well.[18] Bodyweight and bodybuilding forums also discuss semaglutide alongside oral anabolic steroids.[19]

Wikipedia reports the FDA declared a shortage of Ozempic and Wegovy (not Rybelsus) from August 2022, counterfeit Ozempic pens in Europe in October 2023, and a January 2026 estimate by Novo's CEO of up to 1.5 million US users of compounded GLP-1 drugs including semaglutide.[2] Generic semaglutide has been approved or launched in markets including India, Canada and Brazil.[2]
Registered trials examine oral semaglutide in bone turnover, atherosclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, alcohol use disorder and other conditions.[7][8][9][10]

Clinical development has included early-phase trials and phase 3 programmes in type 2 diabetes, summarised in several reviews.[1][3][11] A small retrospective study examined oral semaglutide in diabetic kidney disease.[12]

Phase 3 weight-management trials (OASIS 1 and a 71-week trial of a 25 mg dose),[13][14] the SOUL cardiovascular trial,[15] and an energy-intake and gastric-emptying study[16] are the main published human trials beyond diabetes programmes; a randomised trial in Alzheimer's disease and alcohol-use studies are among registered investigations.[9][10]

timeline.event: Holst and Habener report significant effects of GLP-1.[2]
FDA approves oral semaglutide for weight management (Wegovy) and a cardiovascular indication for Rybelsus.[2]

card.summary: Semaglutide as a daily tablet: proven for type 2 diabetes, with a weight-loss version now approved.
card.note: Boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning; prescription-only.

quick.overview:
Oral semaglutide is the pill version of the GLP-1 drug semaglutide, sold as Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes. An oral version for weight management was approved in the US in December 2025 under the Wegovy name.

Absorption by mouth is low, so it is combined with an absorption enhancer.
quick.mechanism: It activates GLP-1 receptors, affecting appetite and blood sugar. The tablet formulation includes an enhancer that helps absorption in the stomach.
quick.risks: Common effects are nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation. The label carries a boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning, and it is contraindicated with certain thyroid cancer histories.

chain: The tablet activates GLP-1 receptors and reduces appetite
Reduced body weight and body fat, changing facial fullness and body shape
angle.text: Oral semaglutide is an appetite-reducing GLP-1 drug in tablet form. People use it, or the oral weight-management version, to lose body fat, which changes facial and body shape.
